lessons.alt: Top: the classic brigade, from chef de cuisine and sous chef down to six chefs de partie, commis and plongeur. Bottom: the same work shared by a head chef, a hot cook, a cold cook and a porter.
lessons.intro: Every kitchen you walk into still speaks Escoffier, even when nobody wears the titles. He codified the brigade in the early 1900s, borrowing from the army he had served in, and set it down for big hotel kitchens. A full brigade could have more than 20 named roles. Your kitchens will have four to eight people. Knowing the classic map tells you exactly which jobs each of them is quietly doing.

points.p: The chef de cuisine runs the whole kitchen: staff, menus, buying and hygiene. The sous chef is second in command, stands in when the chef is away, and in most kitchens owns rotas, stock and safety. Below them, each chef de partie runs a station. Commis are junior cooks who work a station and report to its chef de partie. The plongeur washes dishes and utensils and may do basic prep. The aboyeur calls orders from the pass to the stations: on your side of the door, that is the expeditor.

The saucier makes sauces and warm starters and finishes meat dishes. The poissonnier cooks fish and seafood. The rôtisseur leads roasting, grilling and frying. The garde manger runs the cold larder: salads, pâtés, terrines and cold starters. The entremetier cooks soups, vegetables and egg dishes. The pâtissier makes desserts, and bread where there is no baker. Each station is a small team with its own mise en place.

Most kitchens now run a reduced version. Fish folds into the sauté section, grill and roast merge into one station, and the staff meal goes to whoever has time. A typical casual restaurant runs a chef, a sous chef, three to five line cooks, a cold larder, a pastry person if needed and a dish pit. As one industry writer puts it, 20 named cooks is too expensive for a 50-seat room. The brigade scales to the room.

In the drawing, the head chef holds chef de cuisine, sous chef and pass. One hot cook covers sauce, fish and roast. One cold cook covers larder, veg and pastry, which is why so many small menus build desserts that can be plated cold. The porter washes and does commis prep. When you plan a menu or a service, count the dishes landing on each person, not each station.

lessons.atWork: At your next pre-shift, ask the head chef who holds which classic station tonight. Write it on the pass. When a table complains about a slow course, you now know which person and which station to ask about, and whether one cook is carrying three sections.
lessons.takeaway: The brigade is a list of jobs, not of people. In a small kitchen, each cook carries several stations, so menu and covers must fit the people.

sources.name: The Kitchen Brigade System and What's Left of It Today, Sobremesa Press

lessons.alt: Waterfall chart: £100 of sales falls by £28 food, £32 labour, £10 rent and £22 other costs, leaving £8 profit. Food plus labour, the prime cost, is £60.
lessons.intro: A full room feels like money. But follow £100 through the till and most of it is gone before anyone sees a profit. This model of a healthy restaurant keeps £8. UK benchmarks put typical net profit at about 3% to 7% of sales, so £8 is a good result, not a modest one. Each line in the waterfall is something a floor manager can move.

points.p: Food cost, the cost of what goes on the plate, is the first bite. One UK accountant's benchmarks put it at 30% to 35% for casual and fine dining and 25% to 30% for pubs with food. Drinks are costed separately, at about 18% to 24% of drinks sales. Waste matters here: it can run at 2% to 10% of food cost, which is money you bought and binned.

Staff costs are the biggest single line. Benchmarks run from 28% to 32% for casual dining and 30% to 35% for fine dining. Food and labour together are called prime cost: here £60 of every £100. Most of the levers you control as a manager sit inside these two lines: rotas, prep, portion control and waste.

Rent and occupancy, including business rates, should usually be 8% to 12% of sales. This is fixed. It is the same whether you do 200 covers or 50, so every extra cover on a quiet night pays for the room that is already rented. When you look at your own site, check this line first: a cheap rent buys room for mistakes everywhere else.

Everything else: energy, insurance, software, repairs, marketing and card fees, which alone can be 1% to 3% of sales. Then profit. One UK guide's worked example of a £1.1m restaurant spends £33 on goods, £30 on staff, £10 on premises and £14 on overheads to keep £13, and calls that a strong year. Note that £100 here means sales after VAT: VAT is the government's money, not yours.

lessons.atWork: Take one week's sales and labour hours. Work out labour as a share of sales for each day. The quietest day will show the highest share. Ask whether one fewer shift, or one more cover per hour, would bring it closer to the 30% band.
lessons.takeaway: From £100 of sales, only about £3 to £8 is profit. Saving £1 on food or labour adds as much profit as roughly £12 to £33 of new sales.

lessons.alt: Guest journey map in seven stages: discover, book, arrive, dine, pay, leave, remember. Touchpoints sit beside each stage. A mood line peaks at dine, dips at pay and ends high at leave.
lessons.intro: A guest's evening does not start at the door or end with the bill. It starts with a search and ends weeks later, when they decide whether to book again. A journey map lays out every moment in between, so you can see where the experience is won and where it quietly leaks. Most of those moments happen before and after the part your team calls service.

points.p: Discover: search results, reviews and your replies, photos, the online menu. Book: the booking page and confirmation. Arrive: greeting, wait and seating. Dine: pacing, refills and check-backs. Pay: bill request, splitting and the card machine. Leave: the farewell. Remember: the review and the decision to return. Common failures are dull: wrong opening hours online, a menu that will not load on a phone, nobody acknowledging a guest at the door, a slow bill.

Draw a line above the stages for how the guest feels. It is never flat. It usually rises through the meal and dips at the edges: the wait at the door, chasing the bill. One US survey of over 1,500 diners found long waits among the top reasons not to visit, and complaints cluster around waiting, not cooking. Waiting is a front-of-house problem.

Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Barbara Fredrickson showed that people judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and how it ended, not by its length. In a 1993 study, most people chose to repeat a longer cold-water trial because its last 30 seconds were slightly warmer. For a restaurant that means two jobs: design one clear high point, and protect the last five minutes. A slow bill can undo a great main course.

lessons.atWork: Stand at the door for the last 20 minutes of service and time three tables from asking for the bill to walking out. If any takes over 5 minutes, fix the pay stage first: card machines on the floor, bills ready on request.
lessons.takeaway: Map the whole journey, then design one peak and a strong ending. Guests remember those two moments far more than the rest.

news.headline: Diners will eat out more in 2027, but they will not queue
news.gist: OpenTable says diners plan to eat out 5 times a month in 2027, and their patience for a queue fell from 29 to 22 minutes.

read.what: OpenTable's 2027 Dining Trends Report says diners plan to eat out 5 times a month, 9 for Gen Z. Dining on OpenTable in the UK rose 10% in 2026 and bookings for 6 or more rose 18%. 67% would rather eat elsewhere than queue, and willingness to queue fell from 29 minutes in 2025 to 22 in 2026.
read.how: Growth comes from small celebrations: reunions (30%), treating themselves (25%) and good news (20%). 36% of Gen Z want to become a regular somewhere in 2027, against 21% of all Brits. Nottingham grew 87% and Sheffield 60%.
read.soWhat: Guests come more often for smaller reasons, and they leave if kept waiting. The arrive stage of the guest journey is where you lose them, and regulars are there to be won.
read.take: Track how long walk-ins wait at the door this week. If it is near 20 minutes, offer a seat at the bar, a drink, or a call-back.

news.headline: Claude Bosi leaves The Peninsula to return to Michelin House
news.gist: Bosi's two-star restaurant at The Peninsula closes in January 2027. He goes back to Michelin House for a new restaurant in spring 2027.

read.what: Claude Bosi has confirmed a new restaurant at Michelin House, 81 Fulham Road, opening in spring 2027. He left the building in 2025 after a falling out with the landlords, then regained the lease. His restaurant at The Peninsula, which won two Michelin stars in about four months, closes in January 2027.
read.how: Bosi and his wife Lucy also run Josephine. Hot Dinners expects a new concept rather than a return of Bibendum, and wonders whether a third Josephine could take the old oyster bar space.
read.soWhat: Even a chef who wins two stars in four months moves when the property deal is right. For your own place, the lease and the landlord shape the business as much as the menu.
read.take: Watch where his team goes. Senior chefs and front-of-house often follow a chef, which can open jobs across London's fine dining scene in the new year.

news.headline: Veeraswamy in court to stay in its home of 100 years
news.gist: Britain's oldest Indian restaurant is fighting the Crown Estate's refusal to renew its £205,000-a-year lease.

read.what: Veeraswamy was due at Central London County Court on 5 November, after a June hearing was postponed. Its £205,000-a-year lease at Victory House ended last summer and the Crown Estate declined to renew. The landlord offered relocation help and £500,000. Owner MW Eat says a move would cost £5m.
read.how: The Crown Estate wants vacant possession to refurbish the building, whose upper offices have been empty since a basement flood in late 2023. MW Eat says works could go ahead while it trades, and has offered to match the rent the landlord expects from offices. A petition of over 20,000 signatures went to Buckingham Palace in February.
read.soWhat: Even a Michelin-starred, 100-year-old restaurant can lose its site when a lease ends. Lease length and renewal terms are among the biggest risks in your own opening.
read.take: When you look at sites, ask what happens at the end of the lease before you ask about the rent. Get a solicitor to check renewal rights.

news.headline: Trade body warns a 5% holiday tax could cost 33,000 jobs
news.gist: A Government bill would let mayors set uncapped visitor levies. UKHospitality says a 5% levy would cost 33,000 jobs by 2030.

read.what: UKHospitality says the Government's bill gives mayors and strategic authorities uncapped powers to tax overnight visitors, without having to spend the money on tourism. Oxford Economics, for the trade body, modelled a 5% levy: 33,000 jobs lost, £1.6bn more tax on holidaymakers, £1.8bn less tourism spending and 11.9 million fewer nights in accommodation.
read.how: Its poll of 10,005 adults found 56% oppose the tax and 24% support it. One in five said it would stop them booking a holiday in England. These figures come from the trade body and its partners.
read.soWhat: A visitor levy hits hotels directly and restaurants indirectly, through fewer visitors. If your site relies on tourists, watch whether your city's mayor plans one.
read.take: Note what share of your covers are hotel guests or visitors. That is the part of your trade a levy would touch.

news.headline: Camille team opens B. Penhale in the old Club Gascon site
news.gist: B. Penhale opens on 16 November at 57 West Smithfield, with 66 covers and regional British and Irish cooking.

read.what: The team behind Camille opens B. Penhale at 57 West Smithfield, the former Club Gascon. Executive chef Elliot Hashtroudi, who named it after his grandmother Betty, leads a menu of regional British and Irish cooking drawn from Victorian recipes. It seats 66, with a walk-in bar and its own menu.
read.how: Whole carcasses are butchered on site. Head of wine Max Hancock is building a list of British and Irish growers and 19th-century grape varieties.
read.soWhat: A walk-in bar beside a booked dining room is a smart way to take spontaneous guests without spoiling the reservations. It answers exactly the queue problem in today's trends story.
read.take: Look at how they split booked tables from walk-in seats. Ask whether your own sites could hold a few seats back for walk-ins.

news.headline: London Museum opens in Smithfield with four places to eat and drink
news.gist: The museum opens on 28 November with a 140-cover bistro, a bar and an alcohol-free cocoa room, curated by Robin Gill.

read.what: London Museum opens in Smithfield on 28 November. Robin Gill is food curator. Clerks House is a 140-cover bistro serving pies and meat-led dishes. Bartholomew's is the bar, with drinks from Mr Lyan Studio. The Temperance Cocoa Rooms, alcohol-free, are open around the clock Thursday to Sunday, and The Roost hosts six-month street food residencies.
read.how: Green & Fortune runs the food and drink on a 10-year partnership.
read.soWhat: Museums and cultural sites are becoming serious dining destinations. An alcohol-free venue open all night is a bold bet on guests who do not drink.
read.take: Visit in its first month and note how a 140-cover bistro handles museum crowds at lunch. Count how many alcohol-free choices the bar offers.

try.title: Time the end of the meal
steps: In the last hour of service, pick three tables and time them from asking for the bill to walking out of the door.
Note where they waited: for the bill, for the card machine, or for coats.
Ask the kitchen which classic stations each cook covered tonight, and whether any dessert held up the last course.
Share the slowest time and one fix at tomorrow's pre-shift.
try.why: Guests judge the night largely by how it ends. A slow bill wastes table time that the £8 of profit depends on, so a faster ending helps both the guest and the margin.

quiz.q: In a four-person kitchen, one cook makes the salads, terrines and desserts. Which classic roles is that cook covering?
quiz.why: The garde manger runs the cold larder (salads, pâtés, terrines) and the pâtissier makes desserts. That is the cold cook in today's drawing.

quiz.q: A table's main course is slow. The hot cook tonight covers sauce, fish and roast. What is the most useful first question?
options: Is the plongeur behind on washing?
Which dishes were on the hot cook at the same time?
Is the sous chef on a break?
quiz.why: In a small kitchen one person carries several classic stations, so a slow course often means one cook had too many dishes at once. Count dishes per person, not per station.

quiz.q: In today's model, food is £28 and labour £32 on £100 of sales. What is prime cost?
quiz.why: Prime cost is food plus labour: £28 + £32 = £60. It is where most of a manager's levers sit.

quiz.q: Net profit is £8 on every £100 of sales. Saving £1 on waste adds as much profit as roughly how much new sales?
quiz.why: At an 8% margin, each £1 of sales leaves 8p profit. To make £1 of profit you need £1 ÷ 0.08 = £12.50 of sales.

quiz.q: A guest has a superb main course, then waits 15 minutes for the bill. What does the peak-end rule predict?
options: They remember the average of the evening
Length of the visit matters most
The slow ending pulls down their memory of the whole night
quiz.why: People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and its end. A poor ending drags down the memory, even after a great peak.

terms.def: A station chef who runs one section of the kitchen, such as sauce, fish or pastry, with commis working under them.
The cold larder station: salads, pâtés, terrines and cold starters.
The kitchen porter who washes dishes and utensils, and may help with basic prep.
Food cost plus labour cost. The largest controllable part of a restaurant's costs, often around 60% of sales.
What is left from sales after every cost, shown as a share of sales. UK restaurants typically make about 3% to 7%.
Any moment a guest meets your business, from a review online to the farewell at the door.
People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and how it ended, not by its length or average.

toolkit.name: Small-kitchen station map
items: Head chef: chef de cuisine, sous chef, pass
Cold cook: garde manger, entremetier, pâtissier
For each person, count the dishes they plate at peak
Write tonight's map on the pass before service

toolkit.name: Where £100 goes
items: Food cost % = food cost ÷ food sales × 100
Prime cost = food cost + labour cost
Profit = sales - food - labour - rent - other costs
Sales needed for £1 profit = £1 ÷ net margin

toolkit.name: Guest journey audit
items: Discover: hours, menu and photos correct on every listing
Book: booking page works on a phone; confirmation sent
Arrive: every guest greeted at once; wait quote honest
Dine: pacing and one check-back per course
Pay: bill within 2 minutes of the request
Leave: a farewell at the door
Remember: reply to every review within a week
